relevance_note: Single-patient case report in which panel NGS 'revealed a nonsense mutation in the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α-induced protein 3 gene, leading to the diagnosis of haploinsufficiency A20 (HA20)' (c.547C>T, p.Arg183*).
method_note: Read the whole paper manually; a Python script in the scratch directory only assembled the JSON and checked spans; no table was machine-transcribed. Table 1 has laboratory variables as rows and time points as columns ('On admission', 'On hospital day 2', 'After 9 months') for the single patient, not patients as columns. Two individuals: the patient (label 'patient'; the paper says 'the patient', 'our patient', and once 'the proband') and 'her father', who has clinical history but was not tested. The mother and younger sister are mentioned only as declining/recommended NGS, with no clinical or genetic information, so they have no rows. Inconsistencies in the paper: the Fig. 1 legend spells the gene 'TNFIP3' while the text says 'TNFAIP3'; the protein change is printed 'p.Arg183^*' in the text and 'p.Arg183*' in the Fig. 1 legend (recorded as 'p.Arg183*'); the sentences 'The c.547C>T variation of the proband was present in our patient' and 'The c.547C>T mutation of the proband was detected in the patient' are ambiguous about who 'the proband' is; treated as one person, the patient. Zygosity and inheritance are not stated (parents refused testing), so both are 'not reported'. '9-year-old' is the age at presentation and the only age given for the reported episode; it is recorded as age at last evaluation (follow-up continued 9 months after colchicine but no age is given then); no explicit age at diagnosis is printed. 'Korea' is the country where the patient was diagnosed ('diagnosed with HA20 in Korea'), not a stated ethnicity. Vital status 'alive' rests on ongoing treatment planning ('Currently, we are considering treatments'). Laboratory values without an interpretation or reference range in the paper (anti-dsDNA IgG 22.6 and 12.8 IU/mL, C3, C4, Hb, platelets, liver and renal tests, and the low WBC values at later time points) were not recorded as features. Checklist choices: 'no uveitis' is recorded as an excluded feature but leaves 'uveitis or other ocular inflammation' not reported (narrow absence); the anal ulcer is recorded as a feature but 'gastrointestinal ulcers or inflammation' is left not reported because the paper groups it with oral and genital mucosal ulcers and does not describe intestinal involvement; the father's 'no history of ... arthritis' leaves 'arthritis or arthralgia' not reported; his tonsillitis is not described as infection, so 'recurrent infections' is not reported. PFAPA criteria and the review figures (89 patients, 26 studies) in the discussion are about other patients and were not attributed to anyone.

treatment_summary.value: Tonsillectomy at 5 years of age (fever then recurred every 3 or 4 months); antipyretics lowered temperature transiently; antibiotic treatment ineffective; colchicine started after HA20 diagnosis, with oral and genital ulcers disappearing after 9 months but fever continuing to recur every 3 or 4 months; immune suppressants such as steroids and biologics (e.g. TNF-α blockers) under consideration.

Colchicine was started, and 9 months after treatment, oral and genital ulcers disappeared. However, the fever continued to recur every 3 or 4 months.

clinical_diagnosis_basis.value: Genetic testing: next-generation sequencing panel for periodic fever and autoinflammatory syndrome genes revealed a nonsense mutation in TNFAIP3, leading to the diagnosis of HA20; testing prompted by clinical features atypical for PFAPA syndrome.
span: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) for genes related to periodic fever and autoinflammatory syndromes was conducted to identify a possible genetic disorder.
It revealed a nonsense mutation in the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α-induced protein 3 gene, leading to the diagnosis of haploinsufficiency A20 (HA20) (Fig. 1).
These features were atypical for PFAPA syndrome; therefore, we performed NGS to identify inflammatory diseases that cause periodic fever.
